PART I

Item 1. Business

We design and manufacture industrial widgets for the aerospace sector. Our customers include the three largest airframe manufacturers. For a discussion of the risks associated with customer concentration, see Item 1A below and the discussion in Item 7.

We operate fourteen plants across nine countries and employ roughly 8,400 people. Revenue is recognised on delivery. Our fiscal year ends on 31 December.

Item 1A. Risk Factors

SENTINEL_1A_START Our business is concentrated: three customers accounted for 62% of revenue in the year, up from 51% in the prior year. The loss of any one of them would materially harm our results of operations.

We depend on a single supplier for the titanium alloy used in our primary product line. We have not qualified a second source, and doing so would take at least eighteen months.

New in this year: our pension obligations have grown materially following a change in the discount rate assumption, and we may be required to make accelerated contributions.

Our products are certified by aviation regulators in each jurisdiction where they are used. Certification of a new part can take three years, and a regulator may withdraw certification of an existing part at any time. Any withdrawal would halt shipments of the affected line and could require us to repurchase inventory already delivered to customers.

We are party to litigation arising from a 2021 plant fire in Cleveland. The plaintiffs seek damages in excess of our insurance coverage. An adverse judgment could exceed our available liquidity and require us to seek additional financing on unfavourable terms, or at all.

Cybersecurity incidents could disrupt manufacturing. In the prior year an intrusion at a supplier halted deliveries to us for eleven days. We have since required suppliers to carry incident response commitments in their contracts, but we cannot verify their controls directly.

Approximately 41% of our workforce is covered by collective bargaining agreements, of which agreements covering 2,900 employees expire within the next twelve months. A work stoppage at the Dayton or Cleveland plants would interrupt production of our highest-margin lines.

We hold significant deferred tax assets whose realisation depends on future taxable income in specific jurisdictions. If forecasts decline, a valuation allowance against those assets would reduce reported earnings, potentially materially, without any change in cash flows. SENTINEL_1A_END

Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments

None.

Item 2. Properties

Our headquarters is in Dayton, Ohio, under a lease expiring in 2031.

PART II

Item 7. Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations

SENTINEL_7_START Revenue increased 4% to $1.42 billion. Gross margin declined 180 basis points to 31.2%, driven primarily by alloy input costs and an unfavourable mix shift toward lower-margin aftermarket parts.

Operating cash flow was $198 million against $241 million in the prior year. The decline reflects working capital build ahead of the Dayton plant expansion.

Selling, general and administrative expense rose 9% to $214 million, of which roughly half relates to the enterprise system implementation begun in the prior year. We expect that programme to conclude in the second half of next year, after which we anticipate the run rate to normalise.

We repurchased 1.4 million shares for $96 million during the year and paid dividends of $61 million. At year end we held $310 million in cash and had $500 million available under our revolving credit facility, which matures in 2029.

Backlog at year end was $1.9 billion, down from $2.1 billion, reflecting the completion of a large aftermarket programme that will not repeat. We expect revenue growth in the low single digits next year. SENTINEL_7_END

Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk

We are exposed to commodity price risk on titanium and aluminium.
